column3: Shares only the qualifier "little"; its limit on human knowledge is otherwise unrelated.
A collective claim of strength and victory contrasts with the obstructers' effort to draw people away from danger.
Its command for upright speech and concern for the vulnerable is only a distant ethical parallel.
God's testing knowledge of those who strive provides a secondary frame for exposing those who hold back.
The immediately preceding verse shows the same people quickly yielding to sedition if the city were entered.
Only shares reported speech; Moses' open summons to Pharaoh does not illuminate internal obstruction.
Hypocrites come to prayer reluctantly, closely paralleling the focus verse's scant participation in danger.
The preceding verse directly continues the exposure of those seeking escape from the threatened community.
Its summons for witnesses uses similar wording but concerns evidentiary claims, not withdrawal from battle.
Directly depicts hypocrites speaking to their brethren and making support promises that their conduct proves false.
Warning against leaning toward wrongdoers is a broad contrast to the obstructers' harmful alignment.
Its restored brotherhood and endurance do not address discouraging others from a common danger.
God knows those who slip away covertly from the Messenger's command, a close parallel to concealed withdrawal.
The verse immediately before the focus recalls their pledge not to turn their backs.
Names Aaron as Moses' brother without the focus verse's obstructive speech or danger.
Directly portrays people who stayed behind and spoke to their brothers to explain deaths away from the fighting.
Its warning about patronal allegiance offers only a distant contrast to true communal support.
The total consumption of inheritance has no meaningful connection beyond a lexical sense of gathering.
God distinguishes those who strive and avoid hidden allegiances, supporting the focus on exposed loyalties.
The prior verse directly rebuts flight from death or killing, the conduct underlying the focus accusation.
Its exception for minor lapses is unrelated to the scant attendance at danger.
The brief duration of worldly life shares only the word "little."
Believers expose people whose emphatic claim to be with them has come to nothing, paralleling unreliable solidarity.
The norm that believers are brothers sharpens how the focus verse corrupts that relationship through harmful urging.
Mutual assistance in an impossible challenge is only a remote collective-action parallel.
Its true patronal support contrasts generally with the focus verse's failed brotherly support.
Lot's fraternal address is not connected to withdrawal or obstruction.
Its praise of covenant-keeping and endurance at the time of battle supplies an affirmative counterpoint.
The call to fight for the oppressed directly supplies the protective purpose from which the obstructers pull others away.
A boast of wealth and supporters does not address communal danger or withdrawal.
Turning away despite a covenant is a broad parallel, but its setting is too general.
It contrasts committed fighting with the opposing camp's schemes, directly relevant to refusal of the contested struggle.
A companion's theological rebuke has no shared scene of collective obstruction.
It directly rejects those who spoke to their brothers about people who traveled or fought, discouraging commitment through regret.
Its command to fight despite death or victory is an immediate counterpoint to staying away from danger.
Calling Shu'ayb their brother only supplies a generic kinship relation.
Its gradual withdrawal of shade and its small measure are unrelated.
God as believers' protector provides a modest contrast to seeking safety through withdrawal and false support.
A travel companion's fatigue is unrelated to the threatened communal front.
The demand for proof against false gods does not illuminate the obstructers' speech.
It joins earnest striving with divine patronage and support, an affirmative counterpart to holding back.
Hud's fraternal warning lacks the focus verse's danger, summons, and obstruction.
Qarun's claim of self-sufficient knowledge is not a close analogue.
It praises emigrants who strove and those who sheltered and helped them, the opposite of internal obstruction.
Appropriate speech in household property care is only a distant verbal parallel.
God's knowledge of goodness in captives is too remote from the focus scene.
The replacement community strives in God's cause without fearing blame, directly contrasting reluctant withdrawal.
A disputed act on a boat does not bear on communal participation in danger.
The universal certainty of death is only a broad backdrop to fear of killing.
Its figurative challenge about divine help does not clarify the obstructers' behavior.
A false claim of divine sonship is unrelated to brother-directed withdrawal.
Its instruction for better debate concerns a different kind of speech and conflict.
Moses' apology within a learning relationship does not parallel evasion of battle.
Breaking the covenant to disclose scripture provides a secondary pattern of withheld duty and breached commitment.
A profession of faith contradicted by reality supplies a general hypocrisy frame for the focus verse.
Communal fragmentation is not specifically obstructing others from a common danger.
Its warning against association in worship is too distant from the immediate social action.
The fate of those who deny and turn away provides a general outcome frame for withdrawal from commanded duty.
False speech made without knowledge is only a broad contrast to truthful disclosure.
A fabricated religious condition does not closely match battlefield obstruction.
Shu'ayb's call to fear God contains no relevant brother-directed conduct.
The brothers' promise to protect their brother belongs to a distinct family narrative.
Speculation about the sleepers' number is unrelated to the focus relationship.
Its brief worldly provision shares only the word "little."
The collective designation "brethren of Lot" does not supply the focus verse's active obstruction.
The end of Noah's opponents' belief is not a close parallel to this scene.
The public accusation around Joseph's brother has no connection to withdrawal from danger.
Joseph's private reassurance of his brother is a contrasting but remote use of brotherhood.
The repeated greeting of peace lacks the focus verse's harmful summons.
Hypocrites perform prayer lazily and only a little, closely matching the focus verse's minimal participation.
A teacher's repeated warning to his student is not a parallel to internal obstruction.
God's knowledge of concealed rejection modestly supports the focus verse's divine exposure of hidden conduct.
Lot's request for help against corrupters lacks the specific brother-directed withdrawal.
The instruction to stand at night except a little is only a lexical overlap.
Brothers become a source of plotting and harm, offering a secondary intra-group betrayal parallel.
Corrupt brethren continually extend one another in error, closely resembling a social bond that amplifies harm.
The divine word of peace is a remote contrast to the focus verse's divisive call.
God's knowledge of what is hidden and disclosed supports the focus verse's exposure, though without its conflict scene.
Its account of defensive struggle to protect worshiping communities gives the threatened front a closely related purpose.
Knowledge of Sabbath violators does not relate to obstructing fighters.
The unchangeability of God's word is not connected to the conduct described here.
God's knowledge of people's movements and resting places is a general counterpart to knowing who attends danger.
The elite's joint accusation against Moses is only a distant instance of hostile speech.
Mocking willing donors exposes hypocritical internal undermining, though the action is not battlefield withdrawal.
Returning on one's tracks after finding a sign is unrelated to evasive retreat.
Directly depicts hypocrites summoned to fight who refuse and speak what is not in their hearts.
The prayer for forgiveness and mercy has no material connection to the obstructers.
The genuinely helpless exemption helps distinguish inability from the focus verse's blameworthy obstruction.
Appropriate speech is only a broad contrast to speech that draws brothers away from duty.
Calling one another brothers while God distinguishes corrupter from reformer provides a modest relational parallel.
Warning against desires that divert people from revelation provides a general frame for being drawn away from duty.
A remembered companion in the hereafter is too remote from the focus scene.
Divine sovereignty over creation does not illuminate internal obstruction.
Confession under punishment is only a distant consequence for wrongdoing.
The curse and sensory deprivation of the condemned do not specify this conduct.
The rule about public evil speech is not a close analogue to urging withdrawal.
The increase of punishment shares only an exception formula.
A question to angels about their mission lacks a relevant social or conflict relation.
Dismissive speech calling revelation ancient tales is a broad parallel to obstructive speech, but in another setting.
Speech that calls to God and is confirmed by righteous action is an affirmative counterpoint to harmful, inactive speech.
The disliked obligation of fighting establishes the duty from which the focus verse's obstructers turn others away.
Those who ask for a king so they may fight, then turn away except for a few, closely prefigures the focus verse's scant participation.
The small company that remains faithful at the river supplies an affirmative counterpart to a larger group's failure under pressure.
It exposes people concerned only with themselves in the aftermath of battle and their false claims about the command.
Those who turned back when the armies met provide a related battlefield-retreat frame.
God's disclosure of what occurred when the two armies met leads directly into the exposure of hypocrites.
The command to take precautions and go forth in groups or all together directly contrasts with obstructing collective mobilization.
It directly describes one among the community who hangs back and treats others' disaster as a benefit to himself.
The laggard regrets not joining only when others receive bounty, revealing opportunistic rather than loyal solidarity.
Those who question why fighting has been prescribed provide a close counterpart to unwillingness before danger.
The command to fight and urge believers on directly answers the focus verse's discouraging summons.
The command not to weaken in pursuing the enemy is a direct counterpoint to reluctance under threat.
Hypocrites wait to align their speech with whichever side gains advantage, paralleling unreliable communal allegiance.
Moses commands his people to enter the holy land and not turn back, making retreat an explicit loss.
The people's fearful refusal to enter despite the command is a close antecedent of withholding oneself from danger.
The two faithful men urge their brethren to enter and trust God, directly reversing the focus verse's harmful summons.
The people tell Moses and his Lord to fight while they remain seated, an exceptionally close parallel to staying back.
Moses' complaint that he controls only himself and his brother registers the communal refusal that precedes it.
Some believers dislike being led out for the true cause, giving a related pre-battle reluctance frame.
Their dispute about the truth as though driven toward death makes the fear behind resistance explicit.
The prohibition on turning backs when meeting the advancing force directly counters flight from the battlefield.
The stated exception confirms that retreat without a tactical purpose is blameworthy in the battle scene.
The command to respond when summoned to what gives life supplies a broad counterpoint to refusing a collective call.
The prohibition on disputing lest courage fail and strength depart closely concerns internal conduct during conflict.
The exhortation to urge believers to fight directly reverses the focus verse's discouragement.
It joins emigration, striving, sheltering, and support in the reciprocal solidarity that the focus verse violates.
It identifies later believers who emigrate and strive as belonging to the community, reinforcing active mutual obligation.
The rebuke for remaining rooted when told to go forth directly addresses reluctance to mobilize.
The warning that God will replace those who do not go forth underscores the consequence of holding back.
The command to go forth whether lightly or heavily equipped is the clearest positive counterpart to avoiding battle.
Their false excuses show speech deployed to evade a costly summons.
The verse distinguishes truthful people from liars who sought leave before their intentions were exposed.
Believers do not ask to be excused from striving with wealth and lives, directly contrasting the focus conduct.
Only those with doubt and wavering hearts ask permission to stay behind.
Their failure to prepare shows that they did not genuinely intend to go out.
Their presence would have increased disorder and sought fitna among the community, closely matching internal obstruction.
Those who earlier sought fitna and tried to overturn the matter provide the wider pattern behind the focus verse.
The request to be left behind, framed as fear of temptation, is a direct example of self-excusing refusal.
Their reaction to believers' good or bad fortune reveals detached and hostile group membership.
Those left behind rejoice at sitting and tell others not to go forth, making the obstructive speech explicit.
The prohibition on future participation follows their prior contentment with remaining behind.
When called to believe and strive, the able among them ask leave to remain with those who stay behind.
Their satisfaction with being left behind explains their sealed, uncomprehending refusal.
The Bedouin excuse-makers provide a related contrast between asserted inability and deliberate lying.
The stated exemption for the weak, ill, and resourceless clarifies why the focus verse's able obstructers are culpable.
The grief of those unable to find transport contrasts sharply with those who seek excuses to avoid going.
Blame falls on the wealthy who ask leave to stay behind, closely defining blameworthy non-participation.
Their post-return excuses continue the pattern of speech used to cover refusal.
Permission to fight because people were wronged supplies the defensive context that makes withdrawal consequential.
Believers seek the Messenger's permission before leaving a collective matter, directly contrasting covert departure.
The arrival of the confederate forces establishes the immediate danger in which the focus obstruction occurs.
The description of fear and shaken assumptions supplies the pressure under which the obstructers act.
The believers' severe testing provides the trial context for distinguishing faithful participation from hypocrisy.
Hypocrites and those with diseased hearts call the divine promise deception, furnishing the adjacent speech of unbelief.
A group tells the people of Yathrib to return and seeks leave to flee, directly parallel to the focus verse's summons.
The next verse continues the portrait of people stingy toward believers and fearful when danger arrives.
It depicts their wish to be out in the desert asking news rather than joining the fighting, an exact continuation.
The Messenger's excellent example supplies the positive model of steadfast response under the same pressure.
Believers recognize the confederates and increase in faith and submission, contrasting the hypocrites' alarm.
Men true to their covenant, including those who fulfilled it, provide the direct opposite of broken commitment and withdrawal.
God rewards the truthful and punishes hypocrites, the outcome frame for the divided responses in this passage.
God repels the confederates and spares believers from fighting, completing the threatened-front narrative.
The warning to hypocrites and city agitators addresses an internal threat akin to obstructing the community during crisis.
When decisive fighting is prescribed, those with diseased hearts look toward death, closely paralleling fear-driven reluctance.
It contrasts reluctant fear with obedience and upright speech once the matter is resolved.
Turning away is linked to spreading corruption and severing kinship, deepening the focus verse's abuse of brotherhood.
Those left behind plead that property and families distracted them, a direct later instance of excuse-making for non-participation.
The left-behind seek to join only when spoils are available, exposing self-interested rather than committed solidarity.
They are called to fight a mighty people and tested by whether they obey, directly returning to the issue of participation.
The explicit exemptions for blindness, lameness, and illness clarify the boundary of culpable absence.
True believers do not doubt and strive with wealth and lives, defining the faithful opposite of the focus conduct.
The rebuke for saying what one does not do directly addresses the gap between brother-directed words and action.
God's abhorrence of saying what one does not do gives that speech-action contradiction an explicit judgment.
The proposed saving exchange prepares the call to costly commitment rather than self-protective withdrawal.
Believing and striving with wealth and lives defines the active fidelity absent from the focus verse.
The command to be God's supporters supplies the affirmative communal role that obstructers refuse.
The hypocrites' spoken testimony is declared false in substance, closely matching exposed speech without inward truth.
Their impressive speech and fearful, self-protective demeanor give a broader portrait of hypocritical internal threat.
They tell others not to support the Messenger's companions so they will disperse, closely paralleling obstructive group-directed speech.
The command to strive against disbelievers and hypocrites recognizes the latter as an internal adversarial force.
